newsitem.title: USA: Florida panel deadlocks on unloading tobacco stock.
newsitem.headline: Florida panel deadlocks on unloading tobacco stock.

text.p: An advisory panel for Florida's pension trustees deadlocked Tuesday over whether to recommend the sale of $835 million worth of tobacco stocks, a state official said.

The issue nows goes before the trustees, including anti-tobacco Gov. Lawton Chiles, who on Jan. 28 will consider selling large holdings of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. and other tobacco stocks in the state's $58 billion employee pension fund.
The seven-member advisory committee was divided over whether to sell the stocks, said Tom Herndon, executive director of the Florida State Board of Administration, which oversees the pension fund.
"It was clear that there was not a consensus or a strong enough sentiment on the issue one way or another," Herndon said.
Some board members said any decision to sell or retain the strongly performing tobacco stocks must have a social dimension.
The debate over tobacco stocks has heated up in recent months as a state lawsuit filed against the industry progressed through a West Palm Beach court.
Florida is seeking more than a billion dollars from cigarette makers for Medicaid health care costs paid by Florida taxpayers for smoking-related illnesses since 1994. A trial is set for August.
Because of Tuesday's deadlock, trust fund staff members will present information to the board of trustees next month without a recommendation.
In effect, the issue has been "bumped upstairs," Herndon said.

In the meantime, the pension fund's investment managers will operate without any new restrictions on stock picking, he said. "As staff we are going to continue to work the way we are now," Herndon said.

A 65-page report, which included the views of outside financial executives, issued earlier this year said tobacco stocks remained a good investment and should remain in the fund covering 725,000 current and former government workers.

Florida has been fighting U.S. tobacco companies for years. Earlier this year, the state's attorney general and the governor proposed divestiture and requested an economic analysis of the consequences of unloading the state's tobacco holdings.
